fields.title: Corrie ten Boom (For Teens)
fields.description: At fifty-one, a Dutch watchmaker named Corrie ten Boom watched six people vanish behind a false wall in her bedroom as the secret police came up the stairs. Her family had hidden Jews from the Nazis; her father died nine days after their arrest, and her sister Betsie died in Ravensbrück. Corrie walked out alive and spent forty years telling the world that God's love is deeper than any pit. This teen edition tells the true story straight: the hiding place and who did not survive it, the camps, the famous scenes checked against the records, and the hard, costly work of forgiveness.

qa.question: Who was Corrie ten Boom?
qa.answer: A Dutch watchmaker, born in Amsterdam in 1892, whose family hid Jews and resistance workers in their house in Haarlem during the Nazi occupation. After a raid in 1944 she was sent to prison and to Ravensbrück concentration camp, where her sister Betsie died. She spent the rest of her life speaking about God's faithfulness and forgiveness in more than sixty countries, and died in California in 1983.

qa.question: Is the book honest about the hard parts?
qa.answer: Yes. It tells how her father died nine days after his arrest, how prisoners were shot and beaten at Vught and Ravensbrück, and how Betsie died. It also says plainly that not everyone in the hiding place survived the war, and that Corrie admitted her own fear, selfishness and struggle to forgive.

qa.question: What does “Jesus is Victor” mean?
qa.answer: It was the motto on a wooden plaque over the fireplace at the Beje on the day of the raid, and Corrie's motto all her life. It looked as if the secret police had won. Her family believed that even then Jesus was the conqueror over every evil power, and she ended her talks with it for decades.

qa.question: Did everyone in the hiding place survive?
qa.answer: No. Six people hid behind the false wall during the raid and were let out two days later. But Mary van Itallie was arrested again within days and murdered at Auschwitz, and the sources disagree about some of the others. Eusie, the cantor, survived the war.

qa.question: How did she treat people who had hurt her?
qa.answer: She worked hard at forgiving them, and said it was hard. She wrote to the man believed to have betrayed her family to tell him she forgave him, pitied women being humiliated by crowds after the war, opened a home for refugees in Germany, and preached to former camp guards. She admitted that small wrongs from friends were sometimes harder to forgive.

qa.question: Was her release really a clerical error?
qa.answer: Nobody knows. She was told years later that it was a mistake, and she believed it. But no document shows an error, her first book written in 1945 never calls it one, and the gas chamber at Ravensbrück began a month after she left, not a week. The danger she escaped was real either way.

qa.question: Where do the stories come from?
qa.answer: From the full-length biography of Corrie ten Boom, which compares her first account written in 1945 with her later books and checks both against independent records such as Dutch war-graves files, the Jewish memorial registers and Yad Vashem. Where a famous scene appears only in her later books, this edition says so.

qa.question: What can a teenager today take from her story?
qa.answer: That courage is built in ordinary habits long before it is needed; that you can open the door to the next person who needs help without seeing the whole road; that God can be near in loneliness and grief; and that forgiveness can start as a decision before the feelings come.

fields.title: A House of Clocks
fields.body_html:
“Pray for the peace of Jerusalem: They shall prosper that love thee.” — Psalm 122:6 (ASV)

In the old centre of Haarlem, a city in the Netherlands, a few steps from the market square and the huge church of St. Bavo, there is a narrow house at Barteljorisstraat 19. From the street it is only one room wide. Behind the shop it climbs and twists: steep stairs, half-landings, rooms at odd levels. The family who lived there called it the Beje (say it “bay-yay”), from the initials of the street name. Today it is a museum, and visitors from all over the world climb those stairs. For more than a hundred years, though, it was just a watchmaker's shop with a family living upstairs.

Corrie ten Boom's grandfather, Willem, opened the shop in 1837. According to the family's records, he started with one hundred guilders. Three generations of ten Booms repaired and sold clocks and watches from that small front room. It is patient, precise work, and it runs on trust. A customer leaves something precious and has to believe it will come back whole and honestly repaired. The ten Booms kept that trust for a century. It would matter more than they could imagine when their neighbours had to trust them with something far more precious than a watch.

Family tradition says that in 1844 Willem heard a sermon on the verse at the top of this chapter and began gathering a small group once a week to pray for the Jewish people and the peace of Jerusalem. No document from 1844 survives to prove the date, and the idea that the prayer went on for exactly a hundred years is a round number for a celebration. But the prayer became part of who the family were. Corrie's father grew up with it, and so did Corrie.

Her father, Casper, set up his own watch shop in Amsterdam as a young married man, in a neighbourhood with many Jewish families. Family tradition says he had close Jewish friends there and sometimes shared their Sabbath meals. That is where Corrie was born, on 15 April 1892, which was Good Friday that year. A lot of popular books say she was born in Haarlem. She wasn't; the records all say Amsterdam. Family tradition adds that she arrived a month early, so small and weak that nobody expected her to live long. She lived to be ninety-one.

Soon after her birth the family moved back to Haarlem to take over the Beje. She was the youngest of five children: Betsie, Willem, Nollie, and a brother, Hendrik Jan, who died as a baby. Over the years three of her mother's sisters came to live there too. With the children, the aunts, the shop, the workroom and a steady stream of visitors, the narrow house was always full. Corrie remembered it as a place where there was always room for one more at the table.

Casper had a phrase for the Jewish people that Corrie never forgot. They were “God's ancient people.” To him, Jews were not a distant religious category. They were neighbours, friends, customers, and fellow lovers of the Scriptures, and God's promises to them still stood.

We usually think courage appears suddenly, in a crisis. The Beje suggests something else. The courage this family would show in 1943 had been growing for a hundred years, in a weekly prayer, an honest trade, and a crowded table. What you practise when nothing is at stake is what you will have when everything is.

One thing to do this week: pick one group of people who are in danger or pushed aside somewhere in the world, or in your own town. Pray for them by name every day this week, the way the ten Booms prayed for Jerusalem every week. Write their name somewhere you will see it each morning.

study_questions.question: Where was Corrie ten Boom born, and why does it matter?
study_questions.answer: In Amsterdam, on 15 April 1892, not in Haarlem as many books say. It is a small correction, but it shows how a famous story can drift into a simpler shape, and why it is worth checking.

study_questions.question: What prayer became part of the ten Boom family's identity?
study_questions.answer: By family tradition, from 1844 Willem ten Boom gathered a group every week to pray for the Jewish people and the peace of Jerusalem, after hearing a sermon on Psalm 122:6.

study_questions.question: How does the Beje show that courage is built over time?
study_questions.answer: The family's later courage grew out of years of ordinary habits: a weekly prayer, an honest trade built on trust, and a house that always made room for one more.

fields.title: Love with Nowhere to Go
fields.body_html:
“God setteth the solitary in families: He bringeth out the prisoners into prosperity” — Psalm 68:6 (ASV)

Corrie's mother, Cor, had been a teacher. In Corrie's memory she was warm and generous, the kind of woman who made up baskets for poor neighbours and remembered every birthday. But she was not strong. A series of strokes left her, by Corrie's account, able to say only a few words. Corrie watched her mother's world shrink to a single room, and saw her love keep coming through the little she could still do. Cor died on 17 October 1921. Corrie was twenty-nine.

Around then came the other great loss of her young life. In her later book The Hiding Place she tells of a young man named Karel, a friend of her brother Willem. She hoped he would marry her. As she remembered it, he visited, walked with her, and seemed to feel the same. But his family expected him to marry someone with money and position, and in the end he did. He came to the Beje to introduce his fiancée.

This story rests completely on Corrie's own memory. No record identifies Karel, and it would be wrong to guess his surname. But listen to what she said happened next. She climbed to her room in misery. Her father came up after her. He didn't tell her to forget Karel. He talked about what to do with love that has nowhere to go: instead of killing it so it stops hurting, she could give it to God and let him send it somewhere else.

Corrie never married. She believed that conversation shaped her whole life. And you can watch the love being redirected. As she told it later, when illness kept Betsie out of the shop, the sisters swapped jobs: Betsie ran the house, and Corrie discovered she loved the workbench. She trained abroad, in Switzerland, and according to the museum, in 1924 she became the first woman in the Netherlands to qualify as a watchmaker. (Other sources say 1921 or 1922, and nobody seems to have seen the certificate.)

She also started clubs for girls, called the Triangle girls, after an emblem whose three sides stood for body, soul and spirit: sport, music, camps and outings alongside Bible study and prayer. From around 1921 she taught the Christian faith to people with intellectual disabilities, whom most churches of the time ignored. The family took in foster children too. None of it made the newspapers. When the war came she was forty-eight, a single woman known around town as the watchmaker's daughter.

Notice two things. First, Corrie's father didn't pretend the heartbreak wasn't real. He just refused to let it make her small. Second, the patient habits of a watchmaker, the organising skills from the clubs, and the trust of hundreds of young people were exactly what the underground would later need. She didn't know she was being prepared. She was just being faithful with what was in front of her.

Maybe something you hoped for has fallen through: a friendship, a relationship, a team, a plan. The easy move is to harden your heart so it stops hurting. The braver move is the one Casper described. Hand the love to God and ask him where it should go now.

One thing to do this week: if there is a disappointment you are carrying, tell God about it honestly in one sentence. Then ask him to show you one person who could use the care you have nowhere to put, and do one kind thing for that person before the week is out.

study_questions.question: What did Corrie achieve as a watchmaker?
study_questions.answer: She trained in Switzerland and, according to the museum, became the first woman in the Netherlands to qualify as a watchmaker, in 1924, though other sources give 1921 or 1922.

study_questions.question: How did her quiet work before the war prepare her for what came later?
study_questions.answer: Watchmaking taught patience and care with small things, the girls' clubs taught her to organise and gave her a network of young people who trusted her, and the foster children taught the family to make room for strangers.

fields.title: A Child at Bedtime
fields.body_html:
“For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time, then will relief and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place, but thou and thy father's house will perish: and who knoweth whether thou art not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” — Esther 4:14 (ASV)

In the early hours of 10 May 1940, German forces crossed the Dutch border. The Dutch army was small and fought bravely for five days. On 14 May German bombers destroyed the centre of Rotterdam, killing hundreds of civilians, and threatened to do the same to other cities. On 15 May the Netherlands surrendered. Queen Wilhelmina and her government had already escaped to London.

At first, ordinary life in Haarlem went on. Shops opened, trains ran, and the ten Booms took in watches for repair. For the Jews of the Netherlands, about 140,000 people, it was a different story. Step by step they were cut off. Jewish civil servants were dismissed. In 1941 every Jew had to register, and later their identity cards were stamped with a large J. They were banned from parks, cinemas, cafés, libraries and public transport. In May 1942 they were ordered to wear a yellow star with the word “Jood” on it. In July 1942 the deportations began, by train from a transit camp called Westerbork, most often to Auschwitz or Sobibor. By the end of the war more than 100,000 Dutch Jews had been murdered, about three out of every four.

What could an old watchmaker do? Casper was in his eighties. Betsie was in her fifties and not strong. Corrie was nearly fifty. They had no weapons, no influence and no money to speak of. When the yellow star came in, Casper meant to go and collect one for himself and wear it beside his Jewish neighbours. His family talked him out of it, since it would only have got him arrested. But his instinct was right. This was not happening to other people. It was happening to God's ancient people, the people the family had prayed for every week.

Corrie's own turning point, as she wrote it down in 1945, was tiny. She was visiting a Jewish doctor one evening when his little girl called down the stairs: he hadn't come up to tuck her in. The doctor went straight up, and Corrie heard him playing with the children before they slept. Sitting there, she realised that the secret police could come for this family any night. Right then, she wrote, she resolved to help the Jews wherever she could.

No vision, no voice. A child wanting to be tucked in, and a woman who decided she could not stand by.

The verse at the top is from Esther. When a powerful official got the Persian king to order the killing of all the Jews, Esther's cousin Mordecai told her two things at once. God does not depend on you: help will come “from another place.” And you are responsible for where God has put you. The ten Booms were not queens. Their position was a watch shop, a narrow house and a lot of friends. Same logic.

Be honest about this part. Most Dutch Christians did not do what the ten Booms did. The penalties were severe and the risks to your own family were real. Most of us would probably have kept our heads down too. That is exactly why this family matters. They weren't unusual people. What set them apart was a settled conviction that their neighbours' lives were their business before God.

Evil rarely asks you to do something monstrous all at once. It asks you to accept one small injustice, then another, and to stay quiet. Where you are right now, at school, online, in your family, may be your “such a time as this.”

One thing to do this week: watch for one moment when someone is being shut out, mocked or treated unfairly and everyone is going along with it. Do one small thing that refuses to go along: sit with them, say something, or tell an adult who can act.

study_questions.answer: At a Jewish doctor's home, she heard his child ask to be tucked in and realised the secret police could take the family any night. She resolved then to help the Jews wherever she could.

study_questions.question: What two things does Mordecai's message to Esther hold together?

fields.title: The Next Person at the Door
fields.body_html:
“Deliver them that are carried away unto death, And those that are ready to be slain see that thou hold back.” — Proverbs 24:11 (ASV)

Nobody at the Beje decided, on a particular day, to join the underground. It happened one knock at a time. In 1941 and 1942 Corrie and Betsie began helping Jews by finding them hiding places in other people's homes, and early in 1942 Corrie joined the organised resistance. Jews who had been warned they were about to be picked up heard, by word of mouth, that the watchmaker's family would help. The family took them in for a night or two, fed them, and went looking for somewhere safer.

The hard part was the “somewhere safer.” Sheltering someone for a night was one thing. Finding a family willing to hide a stranger for months, knowing that discovery could mean prison or death for the whole household, was another. Corrie's 1945 book remembers one night when a Jewish couple, warned they had been betrayed, arrived with nothing. Casper sat with them, because he was good at comforting frightened people. A young helper walked the town all evening looking for an address and found nothing. That night the household took one more burden to God in its evening prayers. A place was found two days later.

By 1943 the Beje was a hub. Around eighty resistance workers visited regularly. Corrie's little room became a kind of exchange where one person's need was matched with another's help. The biggest need was food. Everything was rationed, and you needed a ration card to buy bread or butter. A person in hiding officially didn't exist, so had no card. The underground got cards in large numbers, often in raids on the offices where they were kept, and the Beje became one of the places that passed them on. Corrie's 1945 book catches the pace of it: “Twenty more ration cards? Right, you shall have them.” She kept the stock hidden inside the top step of the staircase, which had been made into a secret cupboard.

All of this raised a real question. The work ran on false names, false papers and false answers to the police. Was it right to lie? In 1943 Corrie's sister Nollie was arrested for hiding a Jewish woman; the records confirm the arrest. In The Hiding Place, written much later, Corrie tells how Nollie refused to lie even then: asked if the woman was Jewish, she said yes. The woman was later rescued by the underground, and Nollie was released after some weeks. Corrie respected her sister, but she did not share her conviction. The work demanded deception, and she practised it. The family did not all agree.

Scripture doesn't settle it in one line either. The Hebrew midwives in Exodus disobeyed Pharaoh's order to kill baby boys, gave him an answer the text doesn't comment on, and God “dealt well with the midwives.” Rahab hid Israel's spies and sent their pursuers the wrong way, and the New Testament praises her faith. Some Christians read that as permission to deceive murderers. Others, like Augustine long ago, held that a Christian must never lie. What was clear to all of them is what Peter told the authorities: “We must obey God rather than men.” Nobody is obliged to help carry out an injustice.

Proverbs 24 has a follow-up line for people who say they didn't know. God, who weighs hearts, knows whether we didn't know or didn't want to. The ten Booms knew enough, and they acted on it.

God rarely shows you the whole road at the start. He shows you the next person at the door. The question for you is probably not whether you'd hide someone from the secret police. It's whether you will open the door to the next person God sends, even when you can't see where it leads.

One thing to do this week: think of one person who has quietly asked for help, or obviously needs it: a new student, a struggling friend, a neighbour. Open the door one step: send the message, offer the help, or invite them in.

study_questions.question: Why were ration cards so important to people in hiding?
study_questions.answer: Food was rationed and could only be bought with a card. People in hiding had no legal existence and so no card, so the underground had to get cards for them, and the Beje became a distribution point.

study_questions.question: How did Nollie and Corrie disagree, according to The Hiding Place?
study_questions.answer: Nollie would not lie even to the police, while Corrie believed the rescue work required deception and practised it. The family respected each other but did not agree.

study_questions.question: What was clear to the ten Booms, whatever they thought about lying?
study_questions.answer: That the laws against the Jews were unjust and no one had to help carry them out: “We must obey God rather than men.”

By 1943 the Beje was a hub. Around eighty resistance workers visited regularly. Corrie's little room became a kind of exchange where one person's need was matched with another's help. The biggest need was food. Everything was rationed, and you needed a ration card to buy bread or butter. A person in hiding officially didn't exist, so had no card. The underground got cards in large numbers, often in raids on the offices where they were kept, and the Beje became one of the places that passed them on. Right, you shall have them.” She kept the stock hidden inside the top step of the staircase, which had been made into a secret cupboard. All of this raised a real question. The woman was later rescued by the underground, and Nollie was released after some weeks. Corrie respected her sister, but she did not share her conviction. The work demanded deception, and she practised it. The family did not all agree. Scripture doesn't settle it in one line either. The Hebrew midwives in Exodus disobeyed Pharaoh's order to kill baby boys, gave him an answer the text doesn't comment on, and God “dealt well with the midwives.” Rahab hid Israel's spies and sent their pursuers the wrong way, and the New Testament praises her faith. Some Christians read that as permission to deceive murderers. Others, like Augustine long ago, held that a Christian must never lie. What was clear to all of them is what Peter told the authorities: “We must obey God rather than men.” Nobody is obliged to help carry out an injustice. Proverbs 24 has a follow-up line for people who say they didn't know. God, who weighs hearts, knows whether we didn't know or didn't want to. The ten Booms knew enough, and they acted on it. It's whether you will open the door to the next person God sends, even when you can't see where it leads. Open the door one step: send the message, offer the help, or invite them in.

fields.title: Seventy Seconds
fields.body_html:
“Thou art my hiding-place; thou wilt preserve me from trouble; Thou wilt compass me about with songs of deliverance.” — Psalm 32:7 (ASV)

By the spring of 1943 people were living at the Beje for weeks and months, and the security police could raid without warning. The family needed a hiding place that could not be found. The man who built it is known only by an alias. Corrie called him Mr. Smit, a well-known architect who worked for the underground. His real name has never been established. He belongs to the huge company of people whose work survives and whose names don't.

He chose Corrie's own bedroom at the very top of the house, the point farthest from the street door, which meant a few precious extra seconds. Along one wall he built a second wall of brick, plastered and aged to look exactly like the old one. The space between was about two and a half metres long and seventy centimetres deep. In front stood a linen cupboard, and under its bottom shelf was a small sliding panel. You crawled through the panel, closed it from inside, and somebody hid it with boxes and linen. Inside there was a grille for air, a mattress, some water and dry biscuits.

The family called it the Engelenbak, the Angels' Crib, after the highest seats in an old Dutch theatre, nearest the angels. It was meant to hide people for hours, not days.

A hiding place is useless if you can't get into it in time, so they practised. Buzzers were wired up so a warning could be given from the shop. Corrie would sound the alarm without notice, often at night, and time everyone with a stopwatch as they raced upstairs, hid every trace of themselves, and crawled through the panel one by one. Their best time, she wrote in 1945, was seventy seconds. Afterwards they went over whatever had given them away. Then Corrie handed out cream puffs.

Over the months, by her count, more than eighty people passed through the house, with never fewer than seven and never more than twelve at a time. Some can now be identified. “Eusie” was Meijer Mossel, a cantor from Amsterdam with a big voice and, as Corrie remembered him, the high spirits of an overgrown boy. “Mary” was Mary van Itallie, who had run a travel agency before the war. What stands out in Corrie's earliest account isn't the fear. It's the life. There was music in the drawing room, a young man playing a violin sonata, and Eusie singing so passionately that Corrie had to warn him the whole street would hear. They ran evening classes: Mary taught Italian, Eusie Hebrew, Hans astronomy, and Casper, well into his eighties, came along with his notebook. The cat was called Maher-shalal-hash-baz, after a name in Isaiah. Underneath it all, Corrie knew the house would be found one day, and she kept a small Bible on her against that day.

But they never mixed up the brick wall and God. The Angels' Crib was well made, and it would do exactly what it was built to do. They knew no wall could finally protect them. Their final hiding place was not something they had built.

One thing to do this week: be practical about one thing you've been avoiding: a conversation, a plan, a deadline. Prepare for it properly. Then do one thing that is simply joyful, with other people, and thank God for it on purpose.

fields.title: Jesus Is Victor
fields.body_html:
“He that dwelleth in the secret place of the Most High Shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty. I will say of Jehovah, He is my refuge and my fortress; My God, in whom I trust.” — Psalm 91:1-2 (ASV)

On Monday, 28 February 1944, Corrie was in bed with flu. Downstairs her brother Willem was leading a Bible study, and the house was busier than usual. Then the alarm sounded. Four Jewish guests and two young resistance workers ran past her bed and into the hiding place. Corrie shoved her own records in after them, hid the panel, and was back in bed when the raiders reached the top of the stairs.

The raid was carried out by the German security police with officers of the Haarlem police. Corrie was arrested at once. When she refused to tell them where the secret room was, they said they would simply watch the house until whoever was inside gave up. Everyone who arrived during the day walked into a trap. The officer in charge questioned Corrie in the shop and hit her across the face again and again. When she cried out to Jesus, he threatened to kill her, and then stopped. Betsie was beaten too. Afterwards Betsie said she pitied the man who had done it.

On the fireplace hung a small wooden plaque that said “Jesus is Victor.” Betsie pointed it out to Corrie, and their father said aloud that it was true. It looked as if the Gestapo had won. Corrie didn't understand what was happening, and she knew that believing is not the same as understanding. When a German noticed a Bible and asked the old man what it said about the government, Casper quoted Peter: “Fear God; honour the Queen.” The officer protested that the Bible said no such thing. Casper politely explained that it said “the king,” but in the Netherlands that meant the Queen. Courtesy, and quiet defiance. As he was led out, he remembered the clock in the hall that needed winding.

How many people were arrested that day is uncertain; the records give numbers from twenty-one to thirty-five. At the police station a mattress was put on the floor for the family. The old man lay down with his children around him, Betsie, Corrie, Nollie and Willem, and his grandson Peter. At his request Willem read Psalm 91, the passage at the top of this chapter, and then Casper prayed. It was the last time, Corrie wrote, that she heard her father pray. The next day, as a bus took them away, people of Haarlem stood silently along the street, many in tears.

Meanwhile, behind the false wall, six people stood in the dark from Monday afternoon until Wednesday, with guards in the house waiting for them. On 1 March policemen friendly to the resistance came on duty, and when it was safe they let them out. The Jews left after dark. Corrie later heard that Eusie was so glad to be outside that he raised his arms in the street and chanted a Jewish prayer.

Many retellings stop there, as if all six were saved. They deserve the truth. Mary van Itallie was arrested again within days at her new address, sent to Westerbork, and murdered at Auschwitz on 1 May 1944. Eusie was betrayed later too, but by the time he reached Westerbork in January 1945 the trains east had stopped, and he survived to become a well-known cantor. The sources disagree about the others.

Read Psalm 91 again in that light. That family read it on the night its protection seemed to fail. They weren't naive. The psalm's deepest promise isn't that nothing bad will ever happen to you. It is that God himself is the refuge, and that he will be with you in trouble. That is the promise the rest of this story tests.

One thing to do this week: read Psalm 91 slowly, all of it. Underline every promise that says God will be with you rather than that nothing will go wrong. Then pray it for someone you know who is going through something hard.

study_questions.answer: They stood behind the false wall from Monday until Wednesday while the house was guarded, and on 1 March sympathetic policemen let them out.

study_questions.answer: No. Mary van Itallie was re-arrested within days and murdered at Auschwitz on 1 May 1944. Eusie survived. The sources disagree about some of the others.

study_questions.answer: He quoted Peter: “Fear God; honour the Queen”, explaining that the Bible says “the king” but in the Netherlands that meant the Queen.

fields.title: Father Was Released
fields.body_html:
“When my father and my mother forsake me, Then Jehovah will take me up.” — Psalm 27:10 (ASV)

The prisoners were taken to the prison at Scheveningen, on the coast near The Hague. The Dutch called it the Orange Hotel, because so many loyal patriots were held there. Casper was so weak the guards had to carry him. Corrie remembered an officer calling him the worst of them all, because he spoke about nothing but Jesus and the Queen. Inside the gate, father and daughter blessed each other, and she looked back at him once. She never saw him again.

Casper ten Boom died on 9 March 1944, nine days after his arrest. The accounts of where he died differ; Corrie was later told his mind had become confused and that he died in a hospital corridor. Fellow prisoners said he stayed brave to the end, saying that if he were freed he would go straight back to helping the Jews. He was buried in a pauper's grave. His children, some of them in the same prison, were not told. He had once said he would count it an honour to give his life for God's ancient people. Now he had.

Corrie was put in a crowded cell, still sick with flu, and a doctor found she had pleurisy. A nurse there quietly slipped her some little booklets of the Gospels. Then she was moved to solitary confinement for weeks. The cell was cold and grey, and she longed for any human face. She was punished for asking about her father and for singing. She went on singing anyway. She made friends with a line of ants on the floor and fed them crumbs. She embroidered her prison clothes with threads pulled from a coloured towel sent from home. Walking alone in the prison garden, a verse steadied her: “And Enoch walked with God.”

At last a letter came from Nollie, who had been released. Gently, it told her their father had lived only ten days after his arrest. Corrie wept for the first time since the raid. The guard she called offered no comfort except to say it was her own fault for breaking the law.

Then came her interrogation. The officer, whom she later named Lieutenant Rahms, surprised her with his courtesy. When he heard about her classes for people with disabilities, he asked whether that wasn't a waste of time. Corrie recognised the voice of the regime in that question. She answered that God's love reaches especially the weak and despised, and that in God's eyes such a person might be worth more than either of them. The next day, she wrote, he told her he hadn't slept for thinking about it, and he confided his own darkness: a family in a bombed German city whose fate he didn't know. Corrie told him there was no darkness Jesus could not drive away. The statement he wrote down, as she remembered it, said she meant to keep helping anyone in need “regardless of their race or creed,” because she was following Christ.

Here is the surprising thing. Corrie's 1945 book says that in that lonely cell she knew a closeness to God she had never known before. God didn't take the loneliness away. He came into it.

Grief and loneliness can be crushing, and they can play tricks on you, telling you that nobody cares and nothing will change. If you are in a dark place like that, please don't sit in it alone. Tell a safe person: a parent, a pastor, a teacher, a doctor, or a crisis line where you live. The psalm's promise is that there is a Father who is never taken away. Often he comes to us through the people we let in.

One thing to do this week: write down the name of one person you could talk to honestly if things got dark, and let them know you're glad they're in your life. If you're struggling right now, talk to them this week.

study_questions.question: How did Corrie learn of her father's death, and how long did he live after his arrest?
study_questions.answer: Through a letter from Nollie in prison. Casper died on 9 March 1944, nine days after the raid, though his children were not told at the time.

study_questions.answer: That God's love reaches especially the weak and despised, and that in God's eyes such a person might be worth more than either of them.

study_questions.question: What did Corrie discover about God in solitary confinement?
study_questions.answer: That he was nearer than she had ever known. He did not remove her loneliness, but he came into it with her.

fields.title: The Back of the Embroidery
fields.body_html:
“When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned, neither shall the flame kindle upon thee.” — Isaiah 43:2 (ASV)

On 6 June 1944, the day Allied armies landed in Normandy, the Germans began emptying the Scheveningen prison. At a small station outside The Hague, in a crowd of prisoners, Corrie saw Betsie for the first time in more than three months. They pushed through until they were in the same railway carriage and sat holding hands, hardly needing to talk. Another woman teased them as “the love-birds.” Whatever came next, they would face it side by side.

The train arrived at four in the morning at Vught, in the south of the country, the only SS concentration camp built on Dutch soil. On the first day the women were made to undress and shower in front of watching soldiers. The sisters held each other and prayed to be spared. Before their turn came, it was stopped, and they were processed privately days later. Corrie always counted that as answered prayer.

With nothing to do all day but sit at long tables, the women began to complain and backbite. Betsie had an idea. She started a society with simple rules: do your best not to grumble, don't speak ill of anyone, speak encouragingly to others. A small group prayed every day that the atmosphere would change. It is a very Betsie idea: small, practical, gentle, and rooted in prayer.

Later Corrie was lined up with older women to be picked for work crews. It felt, she wrote, like a slave market. She had always been independent. Now she told herself she was “in training.” A kind foreman found out she was a watchmaker and put her on testing relay switches for radios, eleven hours a day. On Sunday afternoons there was worship on a patch of grass between two barracks, and soon Corrie was leading it. She also ran a discussion group, like her girls' clubs, and one of her questions was whether the prisoners would have any responsibility towards the defeated enemy after the war. In a Nazi camp in 1944, she was already asking how they would treat the Germans.

She was honest about herself in her letters. Some women around her were heroines who had given up everything on purpose. She was not like that, she wrote. She longed terribly for home. That she had held out at all was only by God's grace.

Vught was still a concentration camp. Men were beaten to death. Prisoners were called out at roll-call and shot minutes later. In early September 1944, with the Allied armies close, the Germans began killing male prisoners before they could be freed. The women stood at the fence and watched men marched out of the gate. Then they heard the shots. Corrie counted one hundred and eighty. She put her head on Betsie's shoulder and asked God why he allowed it.

Afterwards, pouring out her grief, she sensed that she could not and need not carry the sorrows of the whole world. She was to bring them to God and leave them with him. Then she found the picture she would use for the rest of her life. Life, she wrote, looks like the back of a piece of embroidery: a meaningless tangle of threads. That's the underside. One day we will see the right side, and be amazed and thankful. Days later the sisters were packed with some eighty women into a goods wagon with almost no air, and after three days and nights they reached Ravensbrück, north of Berlin.

Isaiah doesn't promise God's people will avoid the water and the fire. He promises God will be with them in it. You're not asked to understand every tangled thread, or to carry the whole world's pain. You're asked to bring it to him.

One thing to do this week: try Betsie's society for seven days: don't grumble, don't speak badly of anyone, and say one encouraging thing to someone every day. Keep a tally of how often you slip, and don't beat yourself up about it.

study_questions.question: What were the rules of Betsie's society at Vught?
study_questions.answer: To do your best not to grumble or complain, not to speak ill of anyone, and to speak encouragingly to others, with a small group praying daily for the atmosphere to change.

study_questions.question: What is the embroidery picture Corrie found at Vught?
study_questions.answer: That life now looks like the back of a piece of embroidery, a tangle of threads, but one day we will see the right side and be amazed and thankful.

study_questions.question: What did Corrie learn on the night of the executions about carrying grief?
study_questions.answer: That she could not and need not carry the sorrows of the whole world herself, but could bring them to God and leave them there.

fields.body_html:
“in everything give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus to you-ward.” — 1 Thessalonians 5:18 (ASV)

When Corrie and Betsie arrived in September 1944 it was already badly overcrowded. The first women they passed were skeletons reaching out for bread. For the first nights the new arrivals had no shelter at all. The sisters cut Betsie's hair short because of the lice, and lay together under one blanket, comforting each other with the psalms. Betsie reminded Corrie that God gives his beloved sleep. Then it rained.

When they were finally processed, everything was taken: clothes, blankets, food. They came out in a thin dress and wooden shoes. But Corrie had hidden their woollen underwear and her small Bible in a corner during the showers, put them on under her dress, and walked past guards who were searching every prisoner. She was not searched. She believed all her life that God had hidden her.

They were moved to Barracks 28. It was built for a few hundred women. By the end, Corrie wrote, it held about fourteen hundred. Bunks were stacked three high, slats were missing, windows were stuffed with rags, and the place crawled with lice. Here, with their hidden Bible, the sisters began what Corrie came to believe was the reason they had been sent there. They held Bible readings every day, sometimes twice. One Sunday Corrie preached nine times, crawling along the top bunks under the ceiling to groups of young women who had asked her to come. Dutch, Belgian, French, Polish and Russian women listened, Protestants and Catholics together. When they had no shared language, the sisters just said the name of Jesus, and faces lit up.

You may know the famous story about the fleas: Betsie insisting they thank God even for the fleas, and the sisters later discovering that the guards stayed out of their barracks because of them, so the Bible readings went on in peace. That story appears in The Hiding Place in 1971. Corrie's 1945 book is a bit different. It mentions lice, and says other women avoided the barracks because of them, and that supervision grew slack as the camp overflowed. Corrie may simply have left the fleas out in 1945, or the story may have sharpened in the retelling. Either way, the lesson was Betsie's. Her whole life in the camp was thanksgiving “in everything.” Notice Paul says in everything, not for everything, as if evil were a gift.

There was also the vitamin bottle. Corrie was allowed to keep a small bottle of liquid vitamins, about half full. She gave drops to the starving women around her every day, and by her account it kept giving for weeks, far longer than it should have, until the women called it the widow's cruse, after the jar of oil that didn't run out for the widow in Elijah's time. When a friend smuggled in a new supply, it ran dry. This story is in her 1945 book, so it wasn't invented later. No one can test it now, and you can judge it for yourself. What isn't in doubt is the other miracle: in a camp where survival seemed to mean looking after yourself, she gave her precious vitamins away every day.

Corrie called that every-woman-for-herself attitude “the Ravensbrück that destroys.” She thought selfishness was more dangerous than cruelty, because it can pass for common sense. She didn't exempt herself. She admitted that once, watching a little birthday feast for a dying girl, she caught herself praying to be offered some, and was ashamed.

Most of us will never be tested like that. But we can practise the habit of looking for God's hand in everything, and giving thanks, and giving first.

One thing to do this week: each night this week, write down three things you can honestly thank God for, including one from inside the hardest part of your day. Then give away something you'd rather keep: time, food, attention, or money.

fields.title: Remember Now, Both of Us
fields.body_html:
“If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: If I make my bed in Sheol, behold, thou art there.” — Psalm 139:8 (ASV)

Betsie ten Boom was nearly seven years older than Corrie, and she was never strong. She never married. For most of her life she kept house at the Beje, kept the shop's books, arranged flowers, and made a shabby old house beautiful on almost no money. She was gentle, orderly and funny. Corrie, lively and impatient, admired her all her life and sometimes felt rebuked by her.

In the camps Betsie became the stronger of the two. Not in body; she was far weaker. But her faith seemed to rest on something the camp could not reach. When a frail Dutch woman was beaten to death in Barracks 28, Corrie turned to Betsie in horror and found her face peaceful. That wasn't indifference. This was the woman who started the society against grumbling, who said the name of Jesus to a lonely Polish prisoner, who pitied the officer who beat her, and who once went to invite a brutal barracks supervisor to the Bible reading. Her compassion was fierce. Evil just didn't seem to get inside her.

Corrie's 1945 book has a line that turns the title of her later book around. Betsie depended on her almost like a child, she wrote, and it was as though Corrie were Betsie's hiding-place in that evil place. The sisters sheltered each other. Corrie gave practical care. Betsie gave a faith that kept her sister from despair.

In the evenings they made plans. When they got home they would open their house to women coming out of the camps. They would make a place in Haarlem for young people whose youth the war had stolen. And the two of them would go to America and tell what God had done.

In the late autumn Betsie became seriously ill. A Dutch nurse got her admitted to the hospital barracks, where she shared a narrow cot with a French girl who kicked her until she fell out. Betsie didn't complain; she said there was such darkness in that poor child's heart, and it was no accident she'd been put beside her. Walking back through the fog, Corrie felt rebellion rising. Why did God leave them there? Why must Betsie suffer? Then, she wrote, she heard three words in French: rempli de tendresse, “filled with tenderness.” Nobody was near. She believed it was God, speaking not to scold her but in love.

Betsie got weaker until she could not walk. As she was carried off to the hospital, a Polish prisoner knelt by her and prayed. That afternoon Corrie visited once more, and as she was sent away Betsie called after her: “Remember now, both of us.” The next morning, looking through the window by her sister's bed, Corrie saw nurses carrying out a body wasted almost beyond recognition. It was Betsie. The date was 16 December 1944. She was fifty-nine.

First came desolation. Then, to her own surprise, peace. Job's words came to her: “Jehovah gave, and Jehovah hath taken away; blessed be the name of Jehovah.” The words most linked with Betsie, that there is no pit so deep that God's love is not deeper still, come from The Hiding Place. Corrie's 1945 book has a related thought in Corrie's own mouth: for those who belong to the Saviour, death is not a pit but a tunnel into the light. Either way, that faith was tested in Ravensbrück, and it held. That night Corrie made room in Betsie's place for a Russian woman nobody would take in.

Losing someone you love can feel like falling into a pit with no bottom. If grief is swallowing you, please tell a safe person: a parent, a pastor, a teacher, a doctor, or a crisis line where you live. The psalm says that even in Sheol, the deepest grave there is, God is already there.

One thing to do this week: think of the person who has most been a “hiding place” for you. Tell them, in a message, a note or face to face, one specific way they have sheltered you.

fields.title: Eight Hours
fields.body_html:
“Our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers: The snare is broken, and we are escaped.” — Psalm 124:7 (ASV)

The day after Betsie died, the whole of Barracks 28 was punished with a roll-call because one woman was missing. They stood in the cold from half past five until noon. At last the missing woman was found: a Polish prisoner, dead in her bunk. The whole barracks had been punished for the absence of a dead woman. Five women, Corrie among them, fell ill after that roll-call, with swollen legs. Within ten days, she wrote, the other four were dead.

Three days after Betsie's death, Corrie's name was called at roll-call. She stepped forward expecting new danger and was told she was being discharged. But released prisoners had to look healthy, and her legs were swollen, so she was sent to the hospital barracks until the swelling went down. That week, she wrote, was among the worst of her imprisonment. At night the sickest women couldn't reach the icy latrine, and some died trying. Corrie helped them, and talked about Jesus as she did.

In one bed lay a young girl named Oelie, who had a learning disability. She was desperately ill and crying for her mother. Night after night Corrie talked to her about the Saviour. On the last night Oelie was able to tell her, simply and in her own words, that Jesus loved her, had taken her punishment, and was preparing a place for her. They thanked God together. Corrie said she understood then why she had been kept that week. The classes for disabled people back in Haarlem had come to this.

One night the windows were thick with frost and the water in the bucket froze solid. The bitter cold had come. In the morning she lay in her bunk listening to thousands of feet stamping outside at roll-call. Weeks earlier she had felt God promise she would be free before the severe cold. She had told the women at the Bible reading that they would all be freed before it came. She had been wrong, she wrote: the promise was for her alone. God, she said, had saved her eight hours before the cold set in.

She walked out with a discharge certificate bearing her prisoner number, 66730. Dutch sources date her release to 28 December 1944. After a hard journey across a collapsing Germany, meeting both cruelty and kindness, she reached a hospital in Groningen. One of the nurses had once been a leader in her girls' clubs and didn't recognise the gaunt woman in front of her. They bathed her and fed her and put her in a real bed. When she heard music again, she wept.

Now a myth to check. For the rest of her life Corrie told audiences that she was released through a clerical error, and that a week later all the women her age were sent to the gas chamber. She learned the “error” years later, apparently on a return visit to Ravensbrück. No document has been found showing a mistake, and her 1945 book never calls it one. Her letters from Vught show the sisters expected their sentence to end on a fixed date, so an ordinary, much-delayed release fits the facts at least as well. And the camp's gas chamber began operating in late January 1945, about a month after she left, not a week. But the danger was real. Sick and old women were already being sent to their deaths, and Corrie, fifty-two and swollen with illness, had every reason to fear the weeks ahead.

Psalm 124 doesn't explain how the snare broke. A bird doesn't know how. It only knows it is free. When she finally reached the Beje in January 1945, her father and sister were gone and much had been stolen. But her piano was there, and her father's chair. She stood by his bed and dared to be happy. She had been given her life back.

One thing to do this week: think of a time you were rescued from something, big or small, even if you don't know how it happened. Thank God for it by name, and tell one person the story.

fields.title: A Letter in June
fields.body_html:
“but I say unto you, Love your enemies, and pray for them that persecute you” — Matthew 5:44 (ASV)

Corrie came home to the Hunger Winter, when food and fuel ran out in the west of the Netherlands and thousands died of hunger and cold. On 5 May 1945 the Germans surrendered. At the first service in the freed Grote Kerk, with a minute of silence for the dead, she found she couldn't sing the national anthem. She named them in her heart: her father, Betsie, and so many others.

In those first days of freedom, crowds all over the country grabbed women accused of relationships with German soldiers, shaved their heads in public and mocked them. Corrie watched from the edge of the crowd and did not join in. One of the girls reminded her of the young women she had known in the camp, and she felt pity, not triumph. She understood why people wanted revenge after five years of humiliation. She was sure this wasn't the way, and she went home.

The war had cost the family terribly. Casper and Betsie were dead. Willem's son Kik, arrested for resistance work, died in Bergen-Belsen in 1945. Willem himself had caught an illness in prison and died in December 1946. The Beje had been plundered.

Then there was the question of who had betrayed them. The Hiding Place tells of a man who came to the shop on the morning of the raid asking for money to free his wife, and names him as the informer, Jan Vogel. That scene isn't in Corrie's 1945 book, which doesn't say how the house was betrayed, and a local historian gives the name differently. You may have read that he was executed after the war. The list of Dutch postwar executions has no one of that name, and without the court records his fate is unknown.

What we do have is a letter. On 19 June 1945, Corrie wrote to the man she had heard was most probably the one who betrayed them. As it was later published, she told him her father had died because of it, and her sister in the camp, and that she had suffered too. Then she told him she forgave him everything. She said she was praying for him and sending him a New Testament, because Jesus had carried his sins and could make him new.

Look at the date. Betsie had been dead six months. The country had been free for six weeks. The grief and anger were raw everywhere. The man hadn't asked for forgiveness. Corrie didn't wait to feel forgiving. Later she liked to say forgiveness is an act of the will, and the feelings follow. This letter is the earliest evidence that she believed it.

Be clear about what she did not do. She didn't pretend he had done nothing wrong; she named exactly what it cost. She didn't ask the courts to let him go. Forgiveness isn't pretending, and it isn't cancelling justice. It is giving up your own claim to pay someone back and handing the debt to God.

And she kept going. She opened a home in Bloemendaal, near Haarlem, for people recovering from the war, as she and Betsie had planned. Her later book says that former collaborators her neighbours despised lived there alongside former prisoners. In 1949 she opened a home for refugees in a former camp in Darmstadt, Germany. (Popular accounts say a concentration camp; the sources don't make clear what kind it was.) She even went to preach to former women guards from Ravensbrück, held in an internment camp. She wrote about it in 1953 in a chapter called “My Chocolate Sermon.”

Most of us are asked to forgive much smaller things. Corrie's example says don't wait until you feel like it. Decide, and act, and trust God to bring the feelings after.

One thing to do this week: if there's someone you need to forgive, write them a letter: name honestly what they did and what it cost you, and then say you forgive them. You don't have to send it yet. Pray over it, and ask a trusted adult whether and how to send it.

study_questions.question: What did Corrie do when crowds shaved the heads of women accused of collaboration?
study_questions.answer: She watched from the edge and didn't join in. She felt pity, recognising in one girl the young women she had known in the camp, and went home.

study_questions.question: What did her letter of 19 June 1945 say to the man believed to have betrayed her family?
study_questions.answer: It named what his betrayal had cost, her father's and sister's deaths, and then told him she forgave him everything, was praying for him, and was sending him a New Testament.

study_questions.question: What does the chapter say forgiveness is not?
study_questions.answer: It is not pretending no wrong was done, and it is not abolishing justice. It is giving up your own claim to repayment and handing the debt to God.

fields.body_text: “but I say unto you, Love your enemies, and pray for them that persecute you” — Matthew 5:44 (ASV) Corrie came home to the Hunger Winter, when food and fuel ran out in the west of the Netherlands and thousands died of hunger and cold. On 5 May 1945 the Germans surrendered. At the first service in the freed Grote Kerk, with a minute of silence for the dead, she found she couldn't sing the national anthem. She named them in her heart: her father, Betsie, and so many others. In those first days of freedom, crowds all over the country grabbed women accused of relationships with German soldiers, shaved their heads in public and mocked them. Corrie watched from the edge of the crowd and did not join in. One of the girls reminded her of the young women she had known in the camp, and she felt pity, not triumph. She understood why people wanted revenge after five years of humiliation. She was sure this wasn't the way, and she went home. The war had cost the family terribly. Casper and Betsie were dead. Willem's son Kik, arrested for resistance work, died in Bergen-Belsen in 1945. Willem himself had caught an illness in prison and died in December 1946. The Beje had been plundered. Then there was the question of who had betrayed them. The Hiding Place tells of a man who came to the shop on the morning of the raid asking for money to free his wife, and names him as the informer, Jan Vogel. That scene isn't in Corrie's 1945 book, which doesn't say how the house was betrayed, and a local historian gives the name differently. You may have read that he was executed after the war. The list of Dutch postwar executions has no one of that name, and without the court records his fate is unknown. What we do have is a letter. On 19 June 1945, Corrie wrote to the man she had heard was most probably the one who betrayed them. As it was later published, she told him her father had died because of it, and her sister in the camp, and that she had suffered too. Then she told him she forgave him everything. She said she was praying for him and sending him a New Testament, because Jesus had carried his sins and could make him new. Look at the date. Betsie had been dead six months. The country had been free for six weeks. The grief and anger were raw everywhere. The man hadn't asked for forgiveness. Corrie didn't wait to feel forgiving. Later she liked to say forgiveness is an act of the will, and the feelings follow. This letter is the earliest evidence that she believed it. Be clear about what she did not do. She didn't pretend he had done nothing wrong; she named exactly what it cost. She didn't ask the courts to let him go. Forgiveness isn't pretending, and it isn't cancelling justice. It is giving up your own claim to pay someone back and handing the debt to God. And she kept going. She opened a home in Bloemendaal, near Haarlem, for people recovering from the war, as she and Betsie had planned. Her later book says that former collaborators her neighbours despised lived there alongside former prisoners. In 1949 she opened a home for refugees in a former camp in Darmstadt, Germany. (Popular accounts say a concentration camp; the sources don't make clear what kind it was.) She even went to preach to former women guards from Ravensbrück, held in an internment camp. She wrote about it in 1953 in a chapter called “My Chocolate Sermon.” Most of us are asked to forgive much smaller things. Corrie's example says don't wait until you feel like it. Decide, and act, and trust God to bring the feelings after. One thing to do this week: if there's someone you need to forgive, write them a letter: name honestly what they did and what it cost you, and then say you forgive them. You don't have to send it yet. Pray over it, and ask a trusted adult whether and how to send it.

fields.title: The Hand Held Out
fields.body_html:
“and hope putteth not to shame; because the love of God hath been shed abroad in our hearts through the Holy Spirit which was given unto us.” — Romans 5:5 (ASV)

This is the most famous story Corrie ever told, so it's worth saying first what kind of evidence it is. It is her own account, and there is no other. The man is never named, and no one else who was there has come forward. It first appeared in print in 1971, more than twenty years after the event, and her 1953 book doesn't mention it. That doesn't mean it didn't happen. It means it reaches us as a memory shaped by many retellings.

As she told it, the year was 1947 and the place a church in Munich, where she had just spoken about God's forgiveness. A man came forward whom she recognised as one of the guards at Ravensbrück, from the place where new prisoners had been processed and humiliated. He didn't recognise her. He said he had since become a Christian and believed God had forgiven him, but he wanted to hear it from one of the women who had suffered there. He held out his hand.

She couldn't take it. She, who had been preaching forgiveness all over Europe, felt nothing but the memory of Betsie in that place. So she prayed silently, telling Jesus she could not forgive this man and asking him to give what she didn't have. Then, as an act of obedience, not feeling, she put out her hand. As their hands met, she said, a warmth of love flowed through her that she knew was not her own, and she could tell him from her heart that she forgave him.

That fits everything else we know. She had written in the camp that she couldn't hate, because she saw her Saviour behind the cruelty. She had written to the informer before she could have felt much at all. And she was honest that forgiveness wasn't a single victory. She said she found Christian friends who wronged her in small ways much harder to forgive than the guard, and that the bitterness kept coming back, so she had to forgive again. Jesus said “Until seventy times seven,” and she found out why.

From 1946 on, she travelled almost without stopping for more than thirty years, speaking in more than sixty countries, including behind the Iron Curtain. Her message was simple: Jesus is the conqueror, God's love is stronger than the deepest darkness, and forgiveness is possible because God gives it. Her motto all her life was the words on the plaque in the Beje: “Jesus is Victor.” In 1971 The Hiding Place made her world-famous, and a film followed. In 1967 Yad Vashem, Israel's Holocaust memorial, honoured her as one of the Righteous Among the Nations, and a tree was planted for her in Jerusalem on 28 February 1968, exactly twenty-four years after the raid. A family that had prayed for Jerusalem for generations was honoured there.

In 1977 she settled in California. On 23 August 1978 a stroke took away most of her speech. For her last five years the woman who had spoken in more than sixty countries could say almost nothing. It echoed her mother's last years, and like her mother she went on loving people through the little she could still do. She died at home on 15 April 1983, her ninety-first birthday.

Her story has two hiding places. The first was the space behind a brick wall, and it saved lives, but it couldn't save everyone. The second was the one she found when the wall could no longer protect her: “Thou art my hiding-place and my shield: I hope in thy word.”

Whom do you find impossible to forgive? Corrie's answer would be simple. Tell God the truth, that you can't. Ask him for his love. And hold out your hand before the feelings arrive.

One thing to do this week: pray this, honestly, about the person you find hardest to forgive: “Jesus, I can't forgive them on my own. Give me your love for them.” Then take one small step of obedience toward them, a greeting, a kind word, or simply refusing to talk badly about them.

study_questions.question: What happened in Munich, according to Corrie?

study_questions.question: Why does the chapter say the Munich story should be told carefully?
